opus-5.5.text:
I think the Epic sepsis model is one of the clearest cautionary tales we have, and it's become a central example in the work Sayash Kapoor and I have been doing on what we call predictive AI.

The basic story is that Epic, which sells electronic health record software to a huge fraction of American hospitals, offered a proprietary sepsis prediction model that hospitals could switch on more or less out of the box. The pitch was that it would flag patients at risk of sepsis early enough for clinicians to step in. Hundreds of hospitals adopted it. But when researchers at the University of Michigan independently evaluated it, it performed far worse than claimed. It missed a large share of sepsis cases, and it fired so many alerts that clinicians would have to sift through a lot of false alarms to find one real case. That feeds alert fatigue, which is a serious patient-safety problem of its own.

A few lessons come out of that.

First, these models often don't transfer across settings. A model trained on data from some hospitals carries assumptions about patient populations, coding practices, and clinical workflows. Deploy it somewhere else and those assumptions can quietly fail. "Plug and play" suggests the model is a neutral tool that works the same everywhere, and in healthcare that's almost never true.

Second, there was leakage in how the model worked. Some of its predictive power seems to have come from signals that reflected clinicians already suspecting sepsis, such as whether antibiotics had been ordered. A model like that looks impressive on paper, but it's partly telling doctors what they already know. It isn't giving them the early warning that justifies its existence.

Third, and this is the bigger structural point, the evaluation was opaque. The model was proprietary, the validation claims came from the vendor, and hospitals mostly lacked the capacity or the access to test it rigorously on their own patients before deploying it. So you had a tool affecting life-and-death decisions at scale with very little independent scrutiny. That's a governance failure as much as a technical one.

What I take from it is not that AI has no role in clinical prediction. It's that the burden of evidence should be much higher than it currently is. Hospitals should validate locally and prospectively, ideally with the kind of rigor you'd expect for a drug or a medical device. Vendors should be transparent about how their models were built and tested. We also need to measure outcomes, not just accuracy. The question isn't whether the model produces a good AUC; it's whether patients actually do better when it's deployed. With the Epic model, even that basic question had largely gone unasked until outside researchers forced it.

r001.rationale: It says the model was proprietary and that hospitals lacked access or capacity to test it rigorously themselves, making scrutiny difficult.

r002.rationale: It reports that University of Michigan researchers found the model performed far worse than claimed, including missing many cases and generating many false alarms.

r003.rationale: It identifies antibiotic orders as a signal reflecting clinicians’ existing suspicion and explicitly describes this as leakage.

r004.rationale: It explains that the model partly tells doctors what they already know and therefore fails to provide the early warning that would justify its use.

r005.rationale: It says models may not transfer across hospitals and recommends local validation, but does not say each hospital should train its own model rather than deploy a shared ready-to-use model.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the Epic sepsis model is one of the most instructive case studies we have, precisely because it wasn't some fly-by-night startup. Epic is the dominant electronic health records vendor in the United States, and this model was deployed at hundreds of hospitals. Sepsis is a huge deal — it's one of the leading causes of death in hospitals, and early detection genuinely matters. So the motivation was sound.

The problem is what happened next. Epic built this model, reported that it performed quite well, and hospitals essentially adopted it as a plug-and-play tool. Then a team at Michigan Medicine did an independent evaluation, and they found that the model's performance was dramatically worse than Epic had claimed. It was missing a large fraction of actual sepsis cases, while also generating alerts on a huge number of patients who didn't have sepsis. So you get alert fatigue on one side and missed cases on the other — kind of the worst of both worlds.

And the deeper issue, which I think is the real lesson here, is about how the model was validated and what information it was actually using. One of the things that came out was that the model appeared to be leaning on signals like whether a clinician had already ordered antibiotics or other interventions. So in effect it was partly "predicting" sepsis after doctors had already started suspecting it — which is not clinically useful. That's a form of leakage, and it's a pattern we see over and over in machine learning: the model looks great on paper because it's picking up on something that is a consequence of the outcome rather than a genuine early predictor.

So what does it reveal about plug-and-play AI in healthcare? A few things. First, there's an enormous gap between a vendor's internal validation and real-world performance across heterogeneous hospitals with different patient populations and different clinical workflows. Second, these models were largely proprietary — hospitals didn't really have visibility into how they worked, and they weren't going through the kind of external validation that we'd demand of a new drug or a medical device. And third, I think it shows that the "deploy and trust" model doesn't work. You can't just drop a predictive tool into a clinical setting and assume it will generalize. You need local validation, you need ongoing monitoring, and you need to be honest about the fact that healthcare data is messy and deeply shaped by human decisions.

The broader point, which Sayash Kapoor and I have been making, is that a lot of the hype around predictive AI rests on evaluations that don't hold up under scrutiny. The Epic case is a vivid example because the stakes were so high and the evidence eventually came out. In many other domains, it never does.

r001.rationale: It says the model was largely proprietary and hospitals lacked visibility into how it worked, limiting their ability to scrutinize it independently.

r002.rationale: It says Michigan Medicine’s independent evaluation found performance dramatically worse than Epic had claimed.

r003.rationale: It identifies clinician orders for antibiotics or other interventions as signals the model used and describes this as leakage.

r004.rationale: It explains that the model was partly predicting sepsis after doctors had already begun suspecting it, making it clinically unhelpful for early detection.

r005.rationale: It recommends local validation and notes differences across hospitals, but does not say each hospital should train the model on its own data.

astra-6.text:
I think it illustrates why we should be skeptical of the idea that you can take a prediction model, drop it into a hospital, and expect better care. The model is only one part of a much larger system. What data does that hospital collect? When does it become available? Who sees an alert, and what can they do in response?

With sepsis, timing is crucial. A model might identify patients who are very sick without giving clinicians useful information early enough to change treatment. And if it generates too many false alarms, it can consume attention that clinicians need elsewhere.

So there are really two questions: Does the model predict accurately in the setting where it’s being used? And does using it actually improve patient outcomes? Those are different questions. The promise of plug-and-play AI tends to obscure that distinction. We need independent evaluation, validation in the local setting, and evidence that the resulting clinical workflow helps patients.

r001.rationale: The response discusses local validation and workflow, but does not say the model is proprietary or that this prevents independent scrutiny.

r002.rationale: It does not mention external validation or performance being worse than Epic claimed.

r003.rationale: It does not identify antibiotic prescriptions as a predictor or describe target leakage.

r004.rationale: It says the model may not provide information early enough to change treatment, but does not explain that clinicians may already have started treatment when the model predicts sepsis.

r005.rationale: It recommends local validation, but does not explain that patient-population differences favor training on each hospital’s own data over deploying one ready-to-use model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it illustrates a fundamental problem with the idea that you can take a prediction model, plug it into a hospital, and assume it will improve care. The model is only one part of a much larger system. You have to ask what data the hospital collects, when those data become available, who sees an alert, and what they can actually do in response.

With sepsis, timing is crucial. A model might appear to predict sepsis, but if it’s picking up on tests or treatments that clinicians have already ordered because they suspect sepsis, it may add very little. And if it generates too many false alarms, it can consume attention and contribute to alert fatigue.

So the question isn’t simply, “How accurate is this model?” It’s, “Does using it lead to earlier, appropriate treatment and better patient outcomes in this particular setting?” That requires independent validation, prospective evaluation, and ongoing monitoring. Plug-and-play marketing tends to obscure how much of that work remains after you buy the software.

r001.rationale: The response discusses plug-and-play limitations but does not say Epic’s model is proprietary or that this prevents independent scrutiny.

r002.rationale: It calls for independent validation but does not report that external validation found worse performance than Epic claimed.

r003.rationale: It mentions tests or treatments generally, but does not identify antibiotic prescriptions as a model predictor or name this as target leakage.

r004.rationale: It explains that when the model relies on tests or treatments clinicians ordered because they already suspect sepsis, it may add little, undermining its value for early detection.

r005.rationale: It recommends evaluation in a particular setting but does not discuss hospital population differences or training a model on each hospital’s own data.
